title: Prompt Sets and Benchmarks — Applied ML Guidelines (2026)
author: Dr. Maya Patel
body:
Overview

This document defines Redwood Inference’s conventions, minimum requirements, and operational playbooks for prompt sets and benchmarks used by the Applied ML & Evals team. It covers: prompt design principles, benchmark construction, metric definitions, integration with the eval harness, model onboarding checklist, quality guardrails, notes for quantization-sensitive benchmarks, and a regression triage playbook.

Goals

- Produce reproducible, human-interpretable prompt sets that capture production-critical behaviors.
- Ensure benchmarks correlate with downstream customer experience (latency-quality-cost trade-offs).
- Provide a repeatable path for model onboarding and automated regression detection + triage.

Principles

1) Representative first, synthetic second: prioritize prompt examples and distributions that reflect customer telemetry and product surfaces. Use synthetic cases to fill coverage gaps only when real data is unavailable or sensitive.
2) Deterministic evaluation: normalize prompts (tokenization, whitespace, RNG seeds) so results are stable across runs.
3) Multi-metric surface: report accuracy/utility + calibration + toxicity/guardrail signals + cost (tokens/us) and latency. A single metric is insufficient.
4) Ownership and lineage: every prompt set must have an owner, creation date, source, and a changelog describing updates.

Prompt set taxonomy

- Customer-derived prompt sets: exported from anonymized telemetry or customer-provided test suites. Required metadata: source_id, data_retention_policy, sampling_query.
- Synthetic perturbation sets: templated transformations to stress failure modes (e.g., instruction negation, hallucination seeds, long-context truncation).
- Edge-case corpora: adversarial or low-resource language samples used for robustness checks.
- Capability probes: short tasks for specific skills (e.g., math, code, summarization) with canonical answers.

Designing a benchmark

Minimum elements (required for any internal benchmark):

- Name (short-dash format), description, owner, created_at, last_updated.
- Prompt set file(s) with canonical prompt, expected outputs (where applicable), and labels.
- Evaluation harness config: model list, temperature/hyperparameters, n_samples, streaming vs non-streaming.
- Metrics list and thresholds (pass/fail & alerting thresholds).
- Runbook: how to execute, where results are pushed, who to notify on regression.

Example benchmark config (human-readable):

- benchmark_name: summarization-production-1k
- sample_source: customer-summaries-prod-2025-06 (anonymized)
- sample_size: 1000
- metrics: ROUGE-L (median >= 0.45), BLEU (median >= 0.12), hallucination_rate (<= 0.05), latency_p95 (<= 250ms on x1-gpu), token_cost_avg (<= 12 tokens/response)

Metric definitions and instrumentation

- Utility metrics:
  - ROUGE-L / BLEU / Exact-match (task dependent). Compute on normalized strings (lowercase, unicode normalize NFKC, strip punctuation unless task requires).
  - HumanEval-style pass@k for code tasks.
- Safety/guardrail signals:
  - Toxicity score (perspective API or internal classifier): report % above threshold and top offending examples.
  - Hallucination detector: binary label + probability; use model-agnostic verifiers when available.
- Calibration & confidence:
  - Expected calibration error (ECE) on classification tasks or predicted-likelihood vs accept rate for generation tasks.
- Cost & latency:
  - token_cost_avg (mean tokens per response * cost_per_token), latency_p50/p95/p99 measured end-to-end in the eval harness environment.

SLOs and alerting thresholds (recommended defaults)

- Major regression: any metric drop > 5% relative on a prioritized benchmark or absolute failure of a critical threshold (e.g., hallucination_rate > 0.1).
- Minor regression: metric drop between 2–5% or isolated increases in latency (p95 increase > 20%).
- Alert routing: major regressions page to applied-ml@redwood.com and #applied-ml-alerts; minor regressions create ticket in Jira with COMPONENT=applied-ml-evals.

Eval harness integration

- All benchmarks must include a harness.yaml that declares:
  - models: list of model_ids to test (e.g., redwood/ggml-7b-q4f16, llama2-13b-8bit)
  - runtime_args: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop_tokens
  - batching_policy: per_model or adaptive
  - seed: integer (for reproducibility)

- Execution steps (runbook):
  1) Checkout eval harness repo and switch to stable tag used by CI (see CI job in .github/workflows/eval.yml).
  2) Place prompt set CSV/JSON in harness/input/ with canonical naming.
  3) Run: ./run_benchmark.sh --config harness.yaml --out results/<benchmark_name>/<timestamp>.json
  4) Post-process: ./tools/aggregate_metrics.py results/... -> results/summary.csv
  5) Upload artifacts to S3://redwood-evals/benchmarks/<benchmark_name>/<timestamp>/ and trigger dashboard refresh.

Model onboarding checklist (applies to new model imports and major version rollouts)

- Pre-ingest
  - Confirm license & acceptable use (legal sign-off).
  - Verify provided model card + architecture notes.
- Basic functionality tests (smoke):
  - Start service in isolation and run 50-sample sanity set: no crashes, outputs non-empty, latency p95 < 2s on standard test GPU.
- Quality evaluation:
  - Run prioritized benchmarks (product-critical suites) and record metrics.
  - Run safety & toxicity checks (edge-case corpora).
- Quantization sensitivity tests (see next section).
- Regression gating:
  - Model must not fail any critical threshold on prioritized production benchmarks. Any failing metric triggers a canary hold and escalation to Applied ML owner.
- Documentation:
  - Add model entry to model-catalog with recommended serving profiles, batch sizes, and quantization profiles.

Quality guardrails and review process

- Guardrail categories:
  - Safety (toxic or disallowed content)
  - Hallucination/Factiveness
  - Reliability (timeouts, OOMs)
  - Cost regressions (tokens, memory)

- Automated checks run on every model push and weekly on production tails:
  - Safety classifier score distribution compared to baseline.
  - Hallucination rate estimate on high-value prompt sets.
  - Canary traffic: 1% of real production routed to new model variant for 24–72 hours before full rollout.

Quantization profile considerations

- Benchmarks should include both FP16/FP32 baseline runs and the target quantized configurations (e.g., q4f16, q8_0). Record delta metrics for each profile.
- Recommended quantization profile table (example):
  - profile_name | target_dtype | expected_mem_reduction | recommended_batch
  - q4f16        | int4+f16       | ~2.8x                 | 8
  - q8_0         | int8           | ~1.9x                 | 12

- Quick checks for quantization suitability:
  1) Latency: ensure p95 does not exceed baseline by >30% for interactive workloads.
  2) Quality: key-task metric delta <= 3% absolute (or relative 5% depending on task criticality).
  3) Failure modes: watch for tokenization edge regressions and increased hallucination on long-context prompts.

Regression triage playbook

1) Detection
  - CI/monitoring alerts or on-call receives notification with link to benchmark result.
2) Initial assessment (within 2 business hours)
  - Owner verifies artifact: compare new results to last-known-good and baseline commit.
  - Check for infra/CI flakiness: rerun benchmark with identical harness.yaml and seed twice.
3) Scoping
  - If reproducible, collect failing examples (top 20) and attach model logs, runtime args, and hardware details.
4) Isolation
  - Run smaller focused tests (ablation): temperature variations, context-length reductions, and different quantization profiles to identify sensitivity.
5) Root cause hypotheses
  - Model change (new weights or patch), tokenization difference, serving runtime change (kernel), quantization regression, or benchmark data change.
6) Remediation
  - If model change: consider rollback to last working candidate and open postmortem.
  - If runtime change: revert kernel or update runtime with a hotfix and rerun tests.
  - If data/benchmark issue: fix prompt normalization or sample selection.
7) Communication
  - Post initial triage: notify stakeholders (applied-ml, platform SRE, product owner) with summary and next steps.
  - For major regressions: create an incident and follow the oncall incident lifecycle.

Appendix A — Example canonical prompt format

Each prompt set row should contain the following columns (CSV/JSON fields):
- id: unique-id string
- source: telemetry | synthetic | partner
- prompt: canonical prompt text (no leading/trailing whitespace)
- context: optional long context blob
- expected_output: optional canonical answer or label
- annotations: comma-separated tags (e.g., "math, low-resource")
- author: owner name

Appendix B — Quick CLI snippets

# Run a single benchmark locally
./run_benchmark.sh --config harness.yaml --prompt-set input/summarization-prod-100.json --models redwood/ggml-7b-q4f16

# Aggregate metrics to CSV
python tools/aggregate_metrics.py --input results/summarization-prod-*/ --output summary.csv

Appendix C — Ownership matrix (examples)

- Benchmark stewardship: Applied ML (owner) + Product (reviewer)
- Safety checks: Applied ML (owner) + Trust & Safety (reviewer)
- CI/infra: Eng infra (owner) + Applied ML (reviewer)

If you have questions or need help converting a product test-suite into an eval benchmark, contact applied-ml@redwood.com or open an RFC with the Applied ML team.
